title: The Majestic-12 documents
notes: Moved from Appendix T's early-record section: the documents surfaced in 1984 through Shandera and Moore, and the data places them with the Kirtland affair, not with 1947. Canon 6 (the named list) extends it.

lead.text: The Majestic-12 documents are papers purporting to show a secret 1950s control group for recovered craft; they surfaced, by the account of their recipients Jaime Shandera and William Moore, as an anonymous roll of film mailed to Shandera in December 1984 and postmarked Albuquerque. The FBI records that an Air Force investigation found the memo it received to be a fake, and the board treats the corpus as evidence about the disinformation of the period rather than about recoveries.

summary.text: According to the Woods' archive, the core corpus, the Eisenhower briefing document and a Truman-Forrestal memorandum, arrived as undeveloped 35mm film addressed to William Moore and Shandera, and everything downstream dates from that delivery; Moore and Shandera controlled the release and published their own analytical report in 1990.

Moore, co-author of the 1980 book The Roswell Incident, later admitted at the 1989 MUFON symposium that he had cooperated with Air Force counterintelligence and passed disinformation to Paul Bennewitz; on the board's reading the film's arrival falls inside the period he admitted.

Stanton Friedman defended the core documents for a decade in Top Secret/MAJIC; Kevin Randle concluded the whole was fabricated. Robert and Ryan Wood's online archive rates the documents' authenticity and argues for much of the corpus.

The corpus spread into the wider retrieval literature: Ryan Wood's 2005 catalogue Majic Eyes Only indexes claimed crash-retrievals with credibility weightings, on the board's reading much of it inherited from Leonard Stringfield's anonymous sources.

record.text: The FBI states that in 1988 two of its offices received versions of a memo titled Operation Majestic-12 claiming to be highly classified, and that an Air Force investigation determined it to be a fake; the Bureau keeps a public file on the documents.

The only document in the National Archives bearing the term MJ-12 is a 14 July 1954 memorandum from Robert Cutler to General Twining, found in Record Group 341; searches of NSC policy papers and minutes for MJ-12, Majestic, UFO, extraterrestrial biological entities and Aquarius found nothing else.

NARA found that the Cutler-Twining memo has no Top Secret register number, sits in a folder with no other MJ-12 material, lacks letterhead or watermark, and carries a marking the NSC FOIA office says was not used until the Nixon administration; its conservation specialist found it a ribbon copy on onionskin.
Moore and Shandera's report The MJ-12 Documents: An Analytical Report (1990) and Moore and Friedman's paper on Klass and MJ-12 (1988) are both cited in the CIA's own 1997 history of its UFO role.
The Air Force's 1995 Roswell report lists Moore's books among the major works it reviewed and records that Friedman began investigating Jesse Marcel's claims in 1978.

The Majestic Documents site is run by Robert M. Wood and Ryan S. Wood, carries a 1999-2026 copyright and publishes an authenticity-ratings scheme alongside FOIA, NARA, Truman Library and British archive sections.
Stringfield wrote seven Status Reports on crash-retrievals between 1978 and 1994, the first delivered at a MUFON symposium.
The State Department's record dates Forrestal as Secretary of Defense from 17 September 1947 to 28 March 1949, a civilian post.

claimed.text: Friedman held that there were no substantive grounds for dismissing the core documents, while himself showing that a purported 17 February 1948 Hillenkoetter memo was an emulation of a published Marshall-to-Roosevelt letter; he won $1,000 from Klass by producing fourteen examples of the typeface used in the Cutler-Twining memo.

The Woods' archive argues for the authenticity of substantial portions of the corpus; Robert Wood, who spent his career at McDonnell Douglas, says he ran a company-funded study of unidentified craft there in the late 1960s.
Majic Eyes Only catalogues claimed crash-retrieval events from the 1940s with dates, places, source trails and numerical credibility weightings.

John Lear's 1987 statement, read aloud on a podcast, says Forrestal was one of several who committed suicide and calls him General Forestall; Jesse Michels, saying he did not know if it was right, suggested Forrestal had heard of recovered bodies shortly before his hospitalisation.
Stringfield himself wrote in his fourth report that public UFO research has no proof and that affidavits, leaked documents and photographs are not proof.

contested.text: Randle concluded the documents were not authentic, and Moore's 1989 admission is his strongest argument; Klass published a forensic critique of the documents' anomalies in 1988. Friedman and Randle's dispute has not been settled by any released record.

On the board's reading, the MJ-12 documents and the Aquarius paper shown at Kirtland in 1983 came from the same Albuquerque channel within twenty months, both through people in contact with AFOSI; this is an inference from timing and contacts.
The Lear document gives Forrestal a military rank that the 1947 Act creating his office forbade, since the Secretary of Defense had to come from civilian life.

On the board's reading, the catalogue's weightings cannot be re-run by a third party and its sources recirculate Stringfield's anonymous informants and the Majestic corpus, so it is an index of claims rather than a ranking.
The board credits the Woods' forensic protocol with making the documents falsifiable, even where its conclusions are wrong, but holds that the corpus's chain of custody disqualifies it.
On the board's reading, McDonnell Douglas's interest in Wood's study would have been corporate self-protection, but no internal record of the study has been released.

questions: Who mailed the film to Shandera in December 1984?
Who were the AFOSI personnel Moore says he worked with, and was he ever given genuine classified material, as he implied?
How did the Cutler-Twining memo come to be in Record Group 341, and who placed it there?
What does Friedman's collection at the Provincial Archives of New Brunswick show about his MJ-12 work?
Does the Navy's 1949 Willcutts board report on Forrestal's death exist in any open archive, and are his medical records sealed?
Which of Stringfield's anonymous informants, if any, were ever named?
